Cheapest first. The page is ordered by how far below the model's expectation the market is pricing a move, on each name's single best horizon. The top of the page is where options cost least relative to what the model thinks is coming; scroll to the bottom for the ones priced richest.

Cheap is not the same as a good trade. An option is often cheap because the market knows something the model does not — a deal closing, a catalyst passing, a stock about to go quiet. The gap is the start of the question.

What a period means. “1 week” is five trading days from the last close — about seven calendar days. “1 month” is twenty-one. The implied move beside it is read from whichever listed expiry falls nearest that horizon, and each row names the expiry it used, so the two are never assumed to be the same date.

What the two bars are. The model's published range is the middle half of outcomes; an option's implied move is a one-standard-deviation move. Those are different units, so the percentages here convert the model's range onto the option's footing — otherwise every stock on the page would look expensive, which would be a unit error rather than a signal.

A gap is a question, not an answer. The market prices things the model cannot see. Whether these gaps predict anything is being recorded daily and has not yet been graded.

How to read the lean. Three inputs, and they are not equal. The model tilt is the only one with a number behind it — measured on 543,000 out-of-sample windows, it calls direction right 51.5% of the time, which is real and small. Options flow is plausible and completely ungraded. Shape says which tail is longer.

When the lean matters. If you are trading the size of the move, only the top half of each row applies — a straddle does not care which way. The lean bears only on choosing one side over the other.

Every input is graded forward, and anything that measures as nothing gets removed rather than quietly kept.
